summary: Denosumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody against RANKL that potently suppresses bone resorption. It is marketed as TWO DISTINCT products with DIFFERENT doses and indications: Prolia (60 mg SC every 6 months) for osteoporosis and bone loss, and Xgeva (120 mg SC every 4 weeks) for prevention of skeletal-related events in bone metastases, giant cell tumor of bone, and hypercalcemia of malignancy. These products are NOT interchangeable. BOXED WARNING (Prolia): patients with advanced chronic kidney disease (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), including dialysis-dependent patients, are at greater risk of severe hypocalcemia, with reported hospitalizations, life-threatening events, and fatal cases; underlying CKD-mineral bone disorder (CKD-MBD) markedly increases this risk. Pre-existing hypocalcemia must be corrected before starting, and all patients require calcium and vitamin D supplementation. Other key risks include osteonecrosis of the jaw (ONJ), atypical femoral fracture, and multiple vertebral fractures after discontinuation.

moa: Denosumab binds with high affinity and specificity to RANKL (receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand), a transmembrane or soluble protein essential for the formation, function, and survival of osteoclasts. By preventing RANKL from activating its receptor RANK on osteoclasts and their precursors, denosumab inhibits osteoclast formation, function, and survival, decreasing bone resorption and increasing bone mass and strength in both cortical and trabecular bone. The effect is reversible: bone resorption markers rise after discontinuation.

Known systemic hypersensitivity to denosumab or any component (reactions have included anaphylaxis, facial swelling, urticaria)
relative: Advanced chronic kidney disease (eGFR <30, including dialysis) - high risk of severe hypocalcemia (boxed warning)
Risk factors for ONJ (invasive dental procedures, cancer, chemotherapy, corticosteroids, poor oral hygiene)
Predisposition to hypocalcemia (hypoparathyroidism, thyroid/parathyroid surgery, malabsorption, small-bowel resection, calcium-lowering drugs)

preg: Prolia is contraindicated in pregnancy. Based on animal data, denosumab can cause fetal harm; in cynomolgus monkeys dosed throughout pregnancy at 50-fold the human dose there was increased fetal loss, stillbirths, postnatal mortality, absent lymph nodes, abnormal bone growth, and decreased neonatal growth. Verify pregnancy status before initiating and advise females of reproductive potential to use effective contraception during therapy and for at least 5 months after the last dose.
lact: There is no information on denosumab in human milk, effects on the breastfed infant, or milk production. Denosumab was detected in maternal milk of cynomolgus monkeys (<=0.5% milk:serum ratio). RANKL-knockout mice showed impaired lactation. Weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and potential infant risk.
renal: No dose adjustment is necessary for renal impairment; pharmacokinetics are unaffected by renal function. HOWEVER, patients with advanced CKD (eGFR <30 mL/min/1.73 m2), including dialysis-dependent patients, are at greatly increased risk of severe, potentially fatal hypocalcemia (boxed warning). Underlying CKD-MBD markedly increases risk. Before initiating, evaluate iPTH, serum calcium, 25(OH) and 1,25(OH)2 vitamin D; monitor serum calcium weekly for the first month then monthly; treatment should be supervised by a clinician experienced in CKD-MBD.
hepatic: No clinical studies have evaluated the effect of hepatic impairment on denosumab pharmacokinetics; no specific dose adjustment is provided.

major: Other denosumab products (e.g., Prolia plus Xgeva or biosimilars) - do NOT use concomitantly; overlapping antiresorptive effect and toxicity
Calcimimetic drugs (e.g., cinacalcet) - may worsen hypocalcemia
moderate: Drugs that lower serum calcium - additive hypocalcemia risk
Immunosuppressants / agents increasing infection risk - may compound serious infection risk
Drugs associated with ONJ (bisphosphonates, antiangiogenics, corticosteroids, chemotherapy) - may increase ONJ risk
minor: No clinically significant effect on CYP3A4 substrates (midazolam) or etanercept pharmacokinetics
interactions.food: Not applicable to the injection; ensure dietary or supplemental calcium 1000 mg and vitamin D >=400 IU daily.
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; encourage good oral hygiene and dental care to reduce ONJ risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Suppresses bone turnover markers (e.g., serum CTX reduced ~85% by day 3); decreases in serum calcium (nadir ~day 10).

counsel: Prolia and Xgeva are different medicines with different doses - never assume they are the same
Take your daily calcium (1000 mg) and vitamin D (at least 400 IU) as directed
Tell your dentist you take this drug; have a dental check-up before starting and keep good oral hygiene to reduce jaw problems
Report new thigh, hip, or groin pain (possible atypical fracture), or numbness, tingling, muscle cramps, or seizures (low calcium)
Seek emergency care for trouble breathing, throat tightness, facial swelling, or hives
Do not stop without a plan - bones can lose strength quickly and spine fractures can occur after stopping; your doctor may switch you to another medicine
If you can become pregnant, use effective contraception during and for at least 5 months after the last dose (Prolia)
pk: Bone resorption marker (CTX) falls ~85% by 3 days; maximal by 1 month
Median Tmax ~10 days (range 3-21 days); Cmax ~6.75 mcg/mL after 60 mg SC
Serum levels decline over 4-5 months; effect reversible (resorption markers rise after stopping)
Refrigerate at 2 C to 8 C in original carton; protect from light; do not freeze; once at room temperature (up to 25 C) use within 30 days; avoid vigorous shaking
pearls: BOXED WARNING: severe hypocalcemia in advanced CKD (eGFR <30) and dialysis patients - can be life-threatening or fatal; CKD-MBD markedly increases risk. Evaluate CKD-MBD and have a CKD-MBD-experienced clinician supervise; monitor serum calcium weekly x1 month then monthly
Prolia (60 mg SC every 6 months) and Xgeva (120 mg SC every 4 weeks) are DIFFERENT products for DIFFERENT indications - do not interchange and never use two denosumab products together
All patients need calcium (1000 mg) plus vitamin D (>=400 IU) daily; correct hypocalcemia before the first dose
Watch for osteonecrosis of the jaw (dental exam before starting) and atypical femoral fracture (thigh/groin pain)
Effect is reversible and not retained in bone - do NOT discontinue without transitioning to another antiresorptive; multiple vertebral fractures have occurred after stopping
Serum calcium nadir occurs around day 10 after a Prolia dose
missed: Prolia: if a 6-monthly dose is missed, administer the injection as soon as the patient is available, then schedule subsequent injections every 6 months from the date of that last injection. Do not simply skip doses - stopping increases the risk of rapid bone loss and vertebral fractures; if therapy is to end, transition to another antiresorptive agent.
overdose: There is no specific antidote; experience with overdose is limited. Excessive RANKL inhibition could deepen hypocalcemia and suppress bone turnover. Monitor serum calcium and provide calcium (oral and/or intravenous) with vitamin D as needed plus supportive care; because of the long half-life (~25 days), monitoring may be prolonged.
